# nish/json

The value of a field, or of several, of one flat JSON object; and `JsonWriter`, which writes any JSON value into a byte buffer.

```ts
import {
  JSON_WRITER_MAX_DEPTH,
  JSON_WRITE_BAD_WINDOW,
  JSON_WRITE_DONE,
  JSON_WRITE_FULL,
  JSON_WRITE_KEY_EXPECTED,
  JSON_WRITE_NON_FINITE,
  JSON_WRITE_OK,
  JSON_WRITE_TOO_DEEP,
  JSON_WRITE_UNBALANCED,
  JSON_WRITE_VALUE_EXPECTED,
  JsonWriter,
  jsonField,
  jsonFields,
  jsonStringifyString,
} from "nish/json";
```

```ts
import { jsonField } from "nish/json";

for (const line of splitLines(stdout)) {
  if (!line.startsWith("{")) {
    continue;
  }
  const code = jsonField(line, "code");
  if (code !== null && code === "NL0003") {
    panic("the compiler crashed");
  }
}
```

<scalar-callout type="info">

The reader exists because the compiler's own machine-readable surface is
JSON: under `--json` every diagnostic is one flat object on a line of
stdout, whose `code` is a stable rule identifier (`AGENTS.md`, and `docs/wp12-release.md` for the
exit-code bands). A Nish program that reads that surface — a wrapper, an
editor plug-in, or `tests/nish/cli.ts`, which pins the contract — needs the
value of a named field and nothing else, and the language has no `JSON.parse`
to give it.

</scalar-callout>

So the reading half is a **reader, not a parser**, and the difference is
worth stating:

- It answers **text**. A string field comes back with its escapes decoded
  and without its quotes; a number, a `true` or a `null` comes back as the
  bytes it was written with, for `parseInt` or `===` at the call site. A
  field whose value is `null` and one whose value is the *string* `"null"`
  therefore answer the same thing, which is the one ambiguity a program that
  needs to tell them apart cannot live with — and the sign that it wants a
  real parser rather than this.
- It answers `null` for a field that is not there, so "absent" and "empty"
  stay apart the way they do in `getenv`.
- It **does not validate**. A nested object or array is stepped over so that
  the fields after it are still reachable, and a truncated object still
  answers the fields that precede the truncation. A program that has to know
  whether the whole line was well-formed is asking a question this does not
  answer.

The reader is two exported functions, and few on purpose. A `std/` module
is compiled into the program that imports it and the symbol namespace is
flat (`std/README.md`), so every name here is a name its importer cannot
use: every helper is `json`-prefixed or a method of `JsonWriter`. Splitting a
stream into lines and picking the ones that start with `{` is two calls the
caller already has — `splitLines` from `std/text` and `startsWith` — and
duplicating them here would cost more names than it saves.

`jsonField` scans from the start of the line on every call, so a caller that
wants three fields of each line reads each line three times. `jsonFields`
reads it once: `jsonFields(line, ["code", "line", "message"])` answers an
array whose slot `k` is exactly what `jsonField(line, names[k])` answers —
absent, first-of-a-duplicate and malformed input included — because the two
share the step that reads one member (`jsonReadMember`) and stop at the same
one. Its array goes back to the caller with the values in it, so a loop that
calls it keeps its per-pass arena release, as one calling `jsonField` does;
`jsonFields`' own comment says when that holds.

<scalar-detail title="The writer">

**The writer** is for the other direction: a server's response body
(WP34 N11, whose first caller is a TechEmpower `/json` entry writing
`{"message":"Hello, World!"}` on every request). `JsonWriter` writes into a
`u8[]` the caller owns and reuses, puts in every comma and colon itself,
and allocates nothing per call except an `f64`'s digits, which it gives back
before the call returns. What it writes is byte for byte what
`JSON.stringify` writes for the same value: the seven short escapes and
`\u00xx` below `0x20`, `/` and `0x7f` as themselves, integers as their
digits, an `f64` as `String(v)` spells it with `-0` as `0`, and NaN and the
infinities as `null`. `jsonStringifyString` is the same string rule
answered as a string.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Two modes">

**Two modes**, both off by default and both kept across `reset`, so a
server sets them once. `setIndent(n)` and `setIndentTab()` write what
`JSON.stringify(v, null, n)` and `JSON.stringify(v, null, "\t")` write:
one member or element a line, `": "` after a key, an empty `{}` or `[]` on
one line, and `n` clamped to 10. The indent is one byte stored as many times
as the depth asks, so the indented text allocates no more than the minified
one, and a `raw` fragment is copied as it is, not re-indented.
`setStrict(true)` makes NaN and the infinities, which JSON cannot
spell, the sticky `JSON_WRITE_NON_FINITE` instead of `null`: for a caller
to whom a `null` where a number was due would be a silently corrupt record.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Misuse is a sticky code">

**Misuse is a sticky code**, as in `nish/net/hpack`: never a panic, and no
`Result` to carry on the hot path. The first call that cannot be honoured
sets `failed` to a negative `JSON_WRITE_*` code — a value where a key is
due, a key where a value is due, an unbalanced or mismatched `end*`,
nesting past `JSON_WRITER_MAX_DEPTH`, a buffer with no room, a second
top-level value, a bad `raw` window or `start`, a non-finite `f64` in strict
mode — and every later call does nothing. A call that fails writes nothing
past `buf.length` (a full buffer is checked before the bytes go in, never
by the bounds check), so the caller writes the whole value, reads `failed`
once at the end, and grows the buffer and retries or answers a 500. `complete()` says whether one
whole value was written with every container closed.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="A string is its bytes">

**A string is its bytes** (WP33 class C, `docs/wp33-round-trip.md` §3.2,
the first row). The writer escapes by byte and copies every byte at or
above `0x80`, so UTF-8 text comes out as the UTF-8 that `JSON.stringify`'s
answer encodes to, and a string that is not UTF-8 — a lone `0xFF` — comes
out raw, where no Node string could hold it in the first place. Under Node
the same source reads UTF-16 units, which agree on ASCII and only there;
`tests/link/std_json_writer` pins both edges natively, and its `node.ts`
is the ASCII half that `tests/run.js` holds to `JSON.stringify` under Node.

</scalar-detail>

Every offset here is a **byte** offset and every width is spelled, with each
length and byte a builtin answers read through `toI32` — `.length` and
`charCodeAt` answer `number`, which is `f64` under `--number-mode f64`, so the
conversion is what makes this one module in both modes rather than two
(`docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §4).

## jsonField

The value of `name` in `object`, or `null` when the object does not have that
field.

A string value comes back unquoted and unescaped; any other value comes back
as the bytes it was written with, so `parseInt` reads a number and `=== "true"`
reads a boolean. The scan is left to right and answers the **first** field of
that name, which is what a duplicated key means to every JSON reader that does
not build a map.

A nested value is stepped over rather than searched, so `name` is a field of
this object and not a path into it: that is the "flat" in the module header,
and it is the shape the compiler's `--json` line has.

```ts
function jsonField(
  object: string,
  name: string,
): string | null
```

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="name" type="string" required>
</scalar-field>

## jsonFields

The value of every one of `names` in `object`, in the order of `names`: slot
`k` is exactly what `jsonField(object, names[k])` answers.

It is for a caller that wants several fields of one line — a diagnostic's
`code`, `line` and `message` — and would otherwise scan the line once per
field. This scans it once, left to right, and stops as soon as every name has
answered: a speed path and nothing more, since a slot is filled only once
and reading on could change no answer. Each slot keeps the **first** field of its name, as `jsonField`
does; a name asked for twice answers in both slots; and a malformed object
answers in each slot what `jsonField` answers for that name, because both
stop at the same member.

The answer is a fresh array and the only allocation besides the values. Each
value is stored into it by a plain `values[k] = text` statement, and the
array is only stored into, tested and returned, so the values travel with
the array: the call lets nothing else out (LANGUAGE.md, "Memory model", a
value stored into an array that is returned with it). A loop calling this
keeps its per-pass release on a line older than the pass, as `jsonField`'s
does, and a `using a = arena()` block may hold the call. On a line built in
the pass neither reader keeps the release (LANGUAGE.md, "Memory model").
Reading `values` back, passing it to a function, or storing it anywhere
before the return would undo this; `tests/link/std_json` pins the flat
arena and the `using` block.

```ts
function jsonFields(
  object: string,
  names: string[],
): (string | null)[]
```

<scalar-field name="object" type="string" required>
</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="names" type="string[]" required>

## jsonStringifyString

`s` as `JSON.stringify(s)` writes it — quoted, with the escapes
`JsonWriter.string` writes — as a string. A thin layer on the writer: it
sizes a buffer to fit exactly, writes into it and reads it back. A string
with nothing to escape skips the writer and is only quoted.

```ts
function jsonStringifyString(s: string): string
```

<scalar-field name="s" type="string" required>

## JsonWriter

A JSON text written into a byte buffer the caller owns: `buf[start ..)`,
up to `buf.length`, with `end` the cursor. Every comma and colon is the
writer's, so the caller says only what the value is:

```ts
const w = new JsonWriter(out, 0)
w.beginObject()
w.key("message")
w.string("Hello, World!")
w.endObject()
if (w.complete()) {
  // out[0 .. w.end) is {"message":"Hello, World!"}
}
```

No call allocates except `f64` (whose digits are a string the call
releases before it returns) and `text`: a writer reset onto the same buffer
for each request keeps `Arena.used()` flat, which `tests/link/std_json_writer`
measures over 10,000 writes.

Misuse is a sticky code, not a panic and not a `Result` (the module header
has the policy). Once `failed` is negative every later call does nothing, so
a caller writes the whole value and reads `failed` once at the end.

```ts
class JsonWriter
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new JsonWriter(buf: u8[], start: i32)` |  |
| `afterKey: boolean` | Whether a key has been written in the innermost object and its value is due. |
| `buf: u8[]` |  |
| `depth: i32` | How many containers are open. |
| `done: boolean` | Whether the top-level value has been written whole. |
| `end: i32` | The cursor: the bytes written are `buf[start .. end)`. |
| `failed: i32` | `JSON_WRITE_OK`, or the first `JSON_WRITE_*` code a call hit. |
| `indentByte: i32` | The byte an indent is made of: a space, or a tab after `setIndentTab`. |
| `indentWidth: i32` | How many `indentByte`s each level of nesting puts at the start of a line, or `0` for the minified text. A mode, not a part of the text: `reset` keeps it, so a writer set up once writes every text the same way. |
| `objectsHigh: i32` |  |
| `objectsLow: i32` | The kinds of the open containers, one bit each, 1 for an object, as a stack 64 bits deep: the innermost is bit 0 of `objectsLow`, an opener shifts the pair left by one and a closer shifts it back. So the check before every value — is the innermost container an object? — is one `and` of one word, and costs the minified text nothing a cached copy would save. Two `i32` words rather than an `i64` or an array, so that a writer allocates nothing and the module still runs under Node, where an `i64` is a BigInt. |
| `sep: i32` | What goes before the next key or element of the innermost container, one `JSON_WRITER_SEP_*`: nothing, a comma, and in an indented text a line break or a comma and a line break. The minified text tests it only where it would test a "comma due" flag, against 0 and 1, so the indented states cost it nothing; bit 1 is the indent and every step keeps it. |
| `start: i32` |  |
| `strict: boolean` | Whether a NaN or infinite `f64` is `JSON_WRITE_NON_FINITE` rather than `null`. Kept by `reset`. |
| `beginArray(): void` |  |
| `beginObject(): void` |  |
| `boolean(v: boolean): void` |  |
| `complete(): boolean` | Whether one whole value has been written, every container closed, and nothing failed. |
| `endArray(): void` |  |
| `endObject(): void` |  |
| `f64(v: f64): void` | `v` as `String(v)` spells it, which is `JSON.stringify`'s rule: the shortest digits that read back as `v`, `-0` as `0`, and `null` for NaN and both infinities, which JSON cannot spell — or, once `setStrict(true)`, `JSON_WRITE_NON_FINITE` for those three, with nothing written. |
| `i32(v: i32): void` |  |
| `i64(v: i64): void` | The digits of `v`, the minimum included: the arithmetic stays on the negative side, where it fits. |
| `key(name: string): void` | The next member's key, with the comma before it and the colon after it. |
| `keyBytes(bytes: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): void` | `key` for a name held as bytes, `bytes[off .. off + len)`, escaped exactly as `key` escapes a string of those bytes, and allocating nothing: what a caller that keeps its text in a byte buffer, such as `nish/json-value`'s `JsonDocument`, writes without making a string per key. A window outside `bytes` is `JSON_WRITE_BAD_WINDOW`, checked once, before anything is written. |
| `nullValue(): void` | `null`. The method is not named `null`, which the parser refuses as a member name. |
| `raw(bytes: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): void` | `bytes[off .. off + len)`, copied as it is and counted as one value: a fragment the caller encoded already, such as a cached object. Nothing in it is checked, so a fragment that is not one whole JSON value makes a text that is not JSON either. The bytes are copied in one move (`copyBytes`), as if all were read before any was written, so a window of the writer's own buffer comes out as it was. In an indented text the fragment goes in where a value would, after its line break and indent, but its own bytes are not re-indented: an object fragment stays on one line, where `JSON.stringify` would spread it out. |
| `reset(buf: u8[], start: i32): void` | Starts a new text at `buf[start ..)`, forgetting everything the last one wrote and every error it hit: what a server calls once per response, on the buffer it reuses. A `start` outside `buf` is `JSON_WRITE_BAD_WINDOW`. |
| `setIndent(spaces: i32): void` | Indents the text by `spaces` spaces a level, as `JSON.stringify(v, null, spaces)` does: each member and element on a line of its own, one space after a key's colon, and an empty `{}` or `[]` left on one line. `spaces` is clamped to 10 as `JSON.stringify` clamps it, and below 1 is the minified text, the default. A mode that `reset` keeps; set it before the text, since a change in the middle of one applies from the next byte. |
| `setIndentTab(): void` | Indents the text by one tab a level, as `JSON.stringify(v, null, "\t")` does. |
| `setStrict(strict: boolean): void` | Whether an `f64` that is NaN or an infinity fails the text with `JSON_WRITE_NON_FINITE`, writing nothing, rather than being written as the `null` `JSON.stringify` writes. Off by default; a mode that `reset` keeps. Strict is for a caller to whom a `null` where a number was due is a corrupt record rather than a missing one. |
| `string(s: string): void` | `s` quoted and escaped as `JSON.stringify` escapes it; every other byte goes through as itself. |
| `stringBytes(bytes: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): void` | `string` for text held as bytes, `bytes[off .. off + len)`: the same quotes and escapes, byte for byte, and no allocation. A window outside `bytes` is `JSON_WRITE_BAD_WINDOW`, checked once, before anything is written. |
| `text(): string` | The bytes written so far, `buf[start .. end)`, as a string. A convenience that allocates a byte at a time, for a caller that wants text rather than bytes; a server sends `buf` itself. |
| `u32(v: u32): void` | One past `i32`'s range is ten digits, so the last digit is split off in `u32` and the nine before it are an `i32`'s. |
| `written(): i32` | How many bytes have been written since `reset`. |

## Limits

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="64" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`JSON_WRITER_MAX_DEPTH: i32`

How deep a writer nests objects and arrays. The kind of each open container
is one bit of two `i32` fields inside the writer, so a nesting past it is
`JSON_WRITE_TOO_DEEP` rather than a stack that grows.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>

<scalar-card title="-2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">
